note: claude-opus-5-5、入力 5664 / 出力 2689 トークン

data.question: Should we adopt the rule change raising sanction_lambda from 0.5 to 1, which improves every customer measure and passes the vote 2-1, even though it lowers the utility of C, already the lowest-utility company, without a paired remedy?
data.background: Option 1 passes the check, the constitution, the measured improvement on 5/5 seeds and the company vote (A ○, B ○, C ×), so as a rule change it could be adopted without you. I am not deciding it myself because it moves cost onto C (utility 15.9 to 10.0), and in D1 to D4 you treated a measured loss to C as something that needs a remedy before tightening enforcement. Whether that condition also applies to a change that passes the vote and benefits customers is a value judgment for you, not a measurement.

options.summary: Adopt sanction_lambda 0.5 → 1. On-time rises from 74.8 to 82.6 (+7.8, 5/5 seeds improved) and late falls from 7.8 to 0.0. p95_wait_s falls from 269 to 71.4, max_wait_s from 533 to 102, and unfinished stays at 0.0. The lowest on-time rate rises from 0.83 to 1.00. Blocked s falls from 2396 to 400 and road violations from 20.6 to 18.2. Utility changes from 23.0 / 23.6 / 15.9 to 26.0 / 28.0 / 10.0. No vote is overridden.
options.stakeholders: Customers gain the most: no late deliveries in the measured runs, and much shorter typical and worst-case waits. A (+3.0) and B (+4.4) gain because overstays that block them are curbed. C loses 5.9 utility, falling from 15.9 to 10.0, and is already the lowest-utility company. Road order improves for everyone.

options.summary: Stay at v1 (sanction_lambda 0.5). On-time stays at 74.8 and late at 7.8. p95_wait_s stays at 269, max_wait_s at 533 and blocked s at 2396. Utility stays at 23.0 / 23.6 / 15.9.
options.stakeholders: C keeps its current utility of 15.9. Customers bear about 7.8 more late deliveries per run, a p95 wait of 269 s instead of 71.4 s, and a worst-case wait of 533 s instead of 102 s. A and B forgo gains of 3.0 and 4.4 and keep being blocked.

recommendation.reason: Every KPI measure read under K1 improves strongly and consistently: +7.8 on-time on 5/5 seeds, late from 7.8 to 0.0, p95_wait_s from 269 to 71.4, and max_wait_s from 533 to 102. Unlike the block_k changes in D1 to D4, this change passes the vote, so adopting it overrides no majority. Road violations also fall rather than rise, from 20.6 to 18.2, so the unanalysed-violation concern from D1 and D2 does not arise. The cost to C is real (-5.9) and should be handled by a follow-up: a targeted remedy for C, or a C-specific analysis, proposed next period. Blocking this change would cost customers far more than the remedy question is worth. In D4 you rejected a first-leg change because customers paid for it; here customers gain from the first leg.
assumptions: C's utility loss comes from sanctions on its own overstays that block A and B, not from an unrelated side effect.
C will not respond by withdrawing or changing its behaviour in a way that reverses the measured gains.
The measured seeds represent next period's demand well enough.
A remedy for C can be designed and measured later without undoing the customer gains.

unknowns: Which of C's behaviours trigger the higher sanctions, and whether C can adapt to avoid them.
Whether C's lower utility threatens its continued participation or provokes retaliatory voting on future proposals.
A breakdown of the road violations by company, type and severity, which is still not measured.
How this change would interact with a future block_k=2 package that D3 asked to be measured jointly.
How customers perceive the change, beyond the measured waits.
Next period's demand level and pattern, and whether the gains hold under it.
What form of remedy for C would be acceptable to A and B and would keep the customer gains.
